content: 1. Individuals receiving antiviral therapy are those who have been diagnosed with chronic hepatitis B infection and have initiated treatment by the end of the reporting period. 2. The numerator is derived from program records, such as clinical records from healthcare facilities providing hepatitis treatment and care. 3. The denominator is sourced from specific program or clinical patient monitoring tools, including electronic or paper medical records, hepatitis testing records, laboratory registers, antenatal care registers, logbooks, and reporting forms at both facility and community levels. 4. Data disaggregation includes age, sex, geographical location, high-risk populations, pregnancy status, HIV infection status, and HDV coinfection status. 5. Treatment outcomes are categorized as died, stopped treatment, or lost to follow-up. 6. The WHO Global Hepatitis Reporting System is used as a global reporting platform. 7. The proportion of people with chronic hepatitis C initiating treatment measures progress toward providing treatment to all eligible individuals with chronic hepatitis C. 8. WHO recommends treatment for all individuals with chronic hepatitis C to achieve a cure. 9. This indicator evaluates the number of people assessed for hepatitis C disease progression, found eligible, and placed on treatment. 10. Disaggregation of data helps assess equity in enrolling specific priority populations. 11. Trends over time reflect progress in treating hepatitis C. 12. If the indicator is measured in a subset of facilities, comments should address the source of information, sample size, and representativeness of all sites delivering hepatitis treatment and care. 13. This indicator is critical for accountability in national health sector strategic plans, effective program management, and donor programming. 14. It is essential for measuring programmatic targets toward eliminating hepatitis C as a public health threat by 2030. 15. The global target is for ≥80% of people diagnosed with chronic hepatitis C to initiate treatment. 16. The numerator includes the number of people diagnosed with chronic hepatitis C who initiated treatment by the end of the reporting period. 17. The denominator includes the number of people diagnosed with chronic hepatitis C with a positive HCV RNA (PCR) or HCV core antigen by the end of the reporting period. 18. Individuals already diagnosed but treated and cured or who spontaneously cleared the infection are excluded. 19. WHO recommends treatment for all eligible individuals with chronic hepatitis B to achieve viral suppression. 20. For those not receiving hepatitis B treatment, WHO recommends annual monitoring for disease progression, ALT levels, and HBV DNA levels. 21. The numerator includes the number of people diagnosed with chronic hepatitis B who are not initiating antiviral therapy but have annual follow-up. 22. The denominator includes the number of people with chronic hepatitis B not initiating treatment. 23. The proportion of attrition from antiviral therapy among people with chronic hepatitis B measures the number of individuals who died, stopped treatment, or were lost to follow-up during the reporting period. 24. WHO recommends treatment for all eligible individuals with chronic hepatitis B. 25. This indicator measures progress in promoting retention on antiviral therapy and mitigating loss (attrition). 26. It is central to understanding total attrition from antiviral therapy during a reporting period. 27. The numerator includes the number of people with chronic hepatitis B reported on antiviral therapy at the end of the last reporting period, plus those newly initiating therapy during the current period, minus those on therapy at the end of the current period. 28. The denominator includes the number of people with chronic hepatitis B reported on antiviral therapy at the end of the last reporting period, plus those newly initiating therapy during the current period. 29. The proportion achieving a cure among people treated for chronic hepatitis C measures the number of individuals who completed treatment and achieved sustained viral response (SVR) at week 12. 30. WHO recommends including information on whether SVR is assessed among all or only a subset of people with chronic hepatitis C and providing the proportion of SVR assessment coverage. 31. The numerator includes the number of people who initiated treatment for chronic hepatitis C and had an SVR test based on HCV RNA testing at 12 weeks after treatment. 32. The denominator includes the number of people who initiated hepatitis C treatment and were assessed for SVR 12 weeks after treatment by the end of the reporting period. 33. The proportion of people with chronic hepatitis B treated and achieving HBV DNA viral suppression measures clinical outcomes, specifically viral suppression among those receiving treatment. 34. Viral suppression is the best available measure of adherence to antiviral therapy and represents the expected outcome of hepatitis B treatment programs. 35. The numerator includes the number of people with chronic hepatitis B receiving treatment for at least one year who have a suppressed viral load (HBV DNA not detectable) based on viral load measurement in the past 12 months. 36. The denominator includes the number of people with chronic hepatitis B receiving treatment for at least one year and assessed for viral load in the past 12 months. 37. The incidence of HBV infection (HBsAg prevalence among children five years or younger) measures the proportion of children with serological evidence of past or present chronic hepatitis B. 38. This indicator describes the reduction in chronic hepatitis B, as most of the disease burden arises from infections acquired before the age of five. 39. Prevention efforts focus on children five years or younger, as they have not yet gone through the high-risk period for chronicity. 40. The United Nations selected the cumulative incidence of chronic hepatitis B at five years of age as an indicator for the Sustainable Development Goal to combat hepatitis. 41. HBsAg estimates the proportion of children with chronic infection likely to develop chronic hepatitis and subsequent sequelae, which is most useful from a public health perspective. 42. Trends in HBV incidence among adults and the general population are reflected through acute hepatitis B surveillance, but these are less informative due to lower chronicity rates in these groups.
